Some of the exegetes said: "Hal" (هَلْ, "has") is in the sense of "qad" (قَدْ, "indeed"). The skilled scholars said: it is on its original basis, a question whose purpose is to stir the listener's soul to receive the news. It was also said: the meaning is, "Did this knowledge come to you except through what We taught you?" In this interpretation there is an affirmation of the blessing. This was said by Sufyan and the majority of the interpreters. Ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-Ghashiyah is the Fire, and Allah the Most High has said: ﴿And the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50], and He said: ﴿And above them will be coverings of Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: its meaning is: toiling in the Fire and weary within it. The "work" here is then the striving of this world. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is: they are toiling in this world and weary in it, because they are not upon guidance, so there is no fruit for their work except fatigue, and its end is the Fire. They said: the verse is about the monks, the idol-worshippers, and every diligent person in disbelief. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, took this approach in interpreting the verse, and he wept out of mercy for a Christian monk whom he saw being diligent. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the Qadariyyah, and he wept and said: among them is the diligent one."

Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Shibl, and Ibn Muhaysin read "ʿāmilah nāṣibah" with the accusative (naṣb) as a form of censure; the verb "naṣib" is implied, its estimate being: "I censure" or "I mean," and similar to this. The Seven and Hafs from ʿAsim, al-Aʿraj, Talhah, Abu Jaʿfar and al-Hasan read "taṣlā" (تَصْلَى) with a fatḥah on the tā' and a sukūn on the ṣād, with the verb in the active voice, i.e., the faces (as subject). Some people read "tuṣallā" (تُصَلَّى) with a ḍammah on the tā', a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the lām, in the sense of transitivity through doubling; Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ transmitted this.

"Al-ḥāmiyah" (الحَامِيَةُ, "intensely hot") is the one kindled and blazing, flaming. "Al-ānIyah" (الآنِيَةُ, "boiling") is the one whose heat has reached its limit, as He the Most High said: ﴿Between it and a boiling hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "ānIyah" is "present for them," from the saying "ana al-shay'" when a thing becomes present.

People differed about "al-ḍarīʿ" (الضَّرِيعُ, "bitter plant"). Al-Hasan and a group of the exegetes said it is al-zaqqum, because Allah the Most High has informed in this verse that the disbelievers have no food except from ḍarīʿ, and He has informed that al-zaqqum is the food of the sinful one. So this requires that ḍarīʿ is al-zaqqum. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ḍarīʿ is stones in the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said: ḍarīʿ is the shibraq (شَبْرَقُ, a thorny plant) of the Fire. Abu Hanifah said: ḍarīʿ is the shibraq, which is a bad pasture on which livestock do not gain fat or flesh. From it is the saying of Abu ʿIzarah al-Hudhali:

"And they were confined in the hazam of ḍarīʿ, so all of them are hunch-backed, bleeding of both hands, with sore..."

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"He grazed on the lush shibraq until it withered, and became ḍarīʿ, from which the fleshy parts became apparent."

The Most High described Paradise as lofty, and this is valid both in terms of distance and place, and also in terms of rank and station.

Others explained it as: "You will not hear in it a group or a company speaking evil." Abu ʿUbaydah said: "lāghiyah" is a maṣdar like al-ʿāqibah and al-jāthiyah. Al-Jahdari read "lā tusmaʿu" with a ḍammah on the tā', and "lāghiyan" with a naṣb. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "lā yasmaʿu" with a yā' below, ḍammah, and "lāghiyah" with a raf'; this is also the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, ʿIsa and al-Jahdari, except that he read "lāghiyah" with a naṣb, in the sense: "No one will hear a lāghiyah word," from your saying "asmaʿtu Zayдan." The meaning is either according to the word or according to the group. The subject of "tasmaʿu" is either the faces, or Muhammad (ﷺ), as al-Hasan said, and you, the addressee, in general. And praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of blessing.

﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming (Event)?﴾ ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled,﴾ ﴿toiling and weary,﴾ ﴿burning in a Fire intensely hot,﴾ ﴿made to drink from a boiling spring,﴾ ﴿they will have no food except from a bitter plant,﴾ ﴿which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.﴾ ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful,﴾ ﴿pleased with their striving,﴾ ﴿in a lofty Garden,﴾ ﴿where they will hear no idle talk.﴾

Some of the exegetes said: "Hal" (هَلْ, "has") is in the sense of "qad" (قَدْ, "indeed"). The skilled scholars said: it is on its original basis, a question whose purpose is to stir the listener's soul to receive the news. It was also said: the meaning is, "Did this knowledge come to you except through what We taught you?" In this interpretation there is an affirmation of the blessing. And "al-Ghashiyah" (the Overwhelming) is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms the whole world with its terror and its alteration of its structure. This was said by Sufyan and the majority of the interpreters. Ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-Ghashiyah is the Fire, and Allah the Most High has said: ﴿And the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50], and He said: ﴿And above them will be coverings of Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. So it covers its inhabitants. The first view is supported by His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled﴾, and the humbled faces are the faces of the disbelievers, and their humbling is their abasement and their being altered by punishment.

People differed regarding His words: "ʿāmilah nāṣibah" (عَامِلَةٌ نَاصِبَةٌ, "toiling and weary"). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: its meaning is: toiling in the Fire and weary within it. Al-nasab (النَّصَبُ) is fatigue, because they were arrogant toward working for Allah the Most High in this world, so He makes them work in the Hereafter in His Fire. ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: the meaning is: toiling in this world and weary on the Day of Resurrection. The "work" here is then the striving of this world. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is: they are toiling in this world and weary in it, because they are not upon guidance, so there is no fruit for their work except fatigue, and its end is the Fire. They said: the verse is about the monks, the idol-worshippers, and every diligent person in disbelief. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, took this approach in interpreting the verse, and he wept out of mercy for a Christian monk whom he saw being diligent. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the Qadariyyah, and he wept and said: among them is the diligent one."

Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Shibl, and Ibn Muhaysin read "ʿāmilah nāṣibah" with the accusative (naṣb) as a form of censure; the verb "naṣib" is implied, its estimate being: "I censure" or "I mean," and similar to this. The Seven and Hafs from ʿAsim, al-Aʿraj, Talhah, Abu Jaʿfar and al-Hasan read "taṣlā" (تَصْلَى) with a fatḥah on the tā' and a sukūn on the ṣād, with the verb in the active voice, i.e., the faces (as subject). Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr (with a variant from him), Abu Rajaʾ, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, and Ibn Muhaysin (and it is differed from Nafiʿ and al-Aʿraj) read "tuṣlā" (تُصْلَى) with a ḍammah on the tā' and a sukūn on the ṣād. This may be from "ṣalaytuhu al-nār" in the sense of "aṣlaytuhu" (I made him burn), so it is like "taḍribu," or it may be from "aṣlaytu," so it is like "takarrama." Some people read "tuṣallā" (تُصَلَّى) with a ḍammah on the tā', a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the lām, in the sense of transitivity through doubling; Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ transmitted this.

"Al-ḥāmiyah" (الحَامِيَةُ, "intensely hot") is the one kindled and blazing, flaming. "Al-ānIyah" (الآنِيَةُ, "boiling") is the one whose heat has reached its limit, as He the Most High said: ﴿Between it and a boiling hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "ānIyah" is "present for them," from the saying "ana al-shay'" when a thing becomes present.

People differed about "al-ḍarīʿ" (الضَّرِيعُ, "bitter plant"). Al-Hasan and a group of the exegetes said it is al-zaqqum, because Allah the Most High has informed in this verse that the disbelievers have no food except from ḍarīʿ, and He has informed that al-zaqqum is the food of the sinful one. So this requires that ḍarīʿ is al-zaqqum. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ḍarīʿ is stones in the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said: ḍarīʿ is the shibraq (شَبْرَقُ, a thorny plant) of the Fire. Abu Hanifah said: ḍarīʿ is the shibraq, which is a bad pasture on which livestock do not gain fat or flesh. From it is the saying of Abu ʿIzarah al-Hudhali:

"And they were confined in the hazam of ḍarīʿ, so all of them are hunch-backed, bleeding of both hands, with sore..."

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"He grazed on the lush shibraq until it withered, and became ḍarīʿ, from which the fleshy parts became apparent."

It was also said: ḍarīʿ is al-ʿashraq. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ḍarīʿ is a thorn in the Fire." Some linguists said: ḍarīʿ is the dryness of al-ʿurfuj when it is broken. Others said: it is the fresh al-ʿurfuj. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a plant like al-ʿawsaj. Some exegetes said: ḍarīʿ is a green, foul-smelling, hollow, elongated plant in the sea, which has a great light in it. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: ḍarīʿ is a tree of Fire. Whoever mentioned any of what we have estimated, he means only that it is of Fire, and necessarily so, and everything in the Fire is fire. Some people said: ḍarīʿ is a valley in Hell. A group of interpreters said: ḍarīʿ is the food of the people of the Fire, and did not intend to specify any of what was mentioned. Some linguists said: this is among what the Arabs do not know. It was said: "ḍarīʿ" is the skin that is over the bone beneath the flesh, and I do not know of anyone who interpreted the verse with this. The people of these sayings say: al-zaqqum is for one group, ḍarīʿ is for another, and al-ghislin is for another.

They differed about the meaning for which it was named ḍarīʿ. It was said: it is ḍarīʿ in the sense of muḍriʿ, i.e., one that weakens the body and emaciates it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the two sons of Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them: "What is wrong with me that I see them ḍāriʿayn?" He means: emaciated. And from faʿīl in the sense of mufʿil is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Yakrib:

"Because of the caller Rayḥanah, the one who hears, my sleeplessness keeps me awake while my companions sleep..."

He means: the hearing (samʿ). It was also said: ḍarīʿ is faʿīl from al-muḍāraʿah, i.e., because it resembles good pasture and resembles it outwardly, though it is not it.

When the Most High mentioned the faces of the people of the Fire, He followed that by mentioning the faces of the people of Paradise, to show the difference. His words "li-saʿyihā" (لِسَعْيِهَا, "with their striving") mean: for their work in this world and their obedience. The meaning is: for the reward of their striving and being blessed for it. The Most High described Paradise as lofty, and this is valid both in terms of distance and place, and also in terms of rank and station.

Nafiʿ alone, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr (with a variant from them), al-Aʿraj, and the people of Mecca and Medina read "lā tasmaʿu fīhā lāghiyah" with a ḍammah on the initial tā' and a raising of "lāghiyah," so some explained it as: "You will not hear in it a lāghiyah word," i.e., one possessing idle talk, so it is in the nisba form. Others explained it as: "You will not hear in it a group or a company speaking evil." Abu ʿUbaydah said: "lāghiyah" is a maṣdar like al-ʿāqibah and al-jāthiyah. Al-Jahdari read "lā tusmaʿu" with a ḍammah on the tā', and "lāghiyan" with a naṣb. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "lā yasmaʿu" with a yā' below, ḍammah, and "lāghiyah" with a raf'; this is also the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, ʿIsa and al-Jahdari, except that he read "lāghiyah" with a naṣb, in the sense: "No one will hear a lāghiyah word," from your saying "asmaʿtu Zayдan." The rest read, and Nafiʿ in the transmission of Kharijah, al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Abu Jaʿfar, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin and Abu ʿAmr (with a variant from him): "lā tasmaʿu" with a fatḥah on the tā' and "lāghiyah" with a naṣb. The meaning is either according to the word or according to the group. The subject of "tasmaʿu" is either the faces, or Muhammad (ﷺ), as al-Hasan said, and you, the addressee, in general. "Al-laghw" (اللَّغْوُ) is the falling of speech, which includes obscenity and all other trivial, deficient speech. There is no deficiency in Paradise, nor any fault in deed or word. And praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of blessing.

﴿Therein is a flowing spring.﴾ ﴿Therein are couches raised high.﴾ ﴿And cups set in place.﴾ ﴿And cushions arranged in rows.﴾ ﴿And carpets spread out.﴾ ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised?﴾ ﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm?﴾ ﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder.﴾ ﴿You are not a controller over them.﴾ ﴿Except for him who turns away and disbelieves.﴾ ﴿Then God will punish him with the greatest punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning.﴾

"'Ayn" (spring) in this verse is an ism jins (a generic noun, a noun denoting a whole class). It is also possible that it is a specific spring, mentioned to honour it. Raising the couches is more honourable for them. "Akwab" (cups) are vessels like the abariq (ewers) that have no handles, no spouts and no lips, and their shape is well known among the Arabs. The phrase "mawdu'a" (placed) means: prepared with their drinks. "Namaraqa" is a cushion, and it is said "numruqa" with a kasra on the nun and the ra'. Zuhayr said:

"Elders and youths, handsome of face, on couches and cushions arranged in rows."

[p. 601] "Zarabi" (carpets), whose singular is "zarbiyya," and it is said with a fatha on the za', are like tanafis (rugs) that have a pile. This is the view of al-Farra'. They are multicoloured. The phrase "mabthuthah" (spread out) means: abundant and scattered.

Then God, exalted is He, established the proof against those who denied His power to resurrect bodies, by making them stand before the place of reflection in His creation. "Al-ibil" (camels) in this verse are the well-known camels. This is the view of the majority of the interpreters. In camels there are signs and lessons for whoever reflects. Among animals, none other than it rises up with a load while kneeling, and despite its strength it is extremely submissive. Al-Tha'labi said in some tafsirs (exegetical works): a mouse pulled the halter of a she-camel and followed it until it entered its hole, and the she-camel knelt down and lowered her head to the mouth of the hole. Shurayh the judge used to say to his companions: "Come out with us to al-Kunasa until we look at the camels, how they were created." Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: "Al-ibil here means the clouds, because the Arabs sometimes call them by this name, since they come in herds like camels and are driven as camels are driven, and in their form they sometimes resemble camels and ostriches." From this is the saying of the poet:

"As if the clouds below the sky are ostriches hanging by their legs."

Abu 'Amr, in one of the reported readings, and 'Isa read "al-ibbil" with a shadda on the lam, meaning the clouds, according to what some lexicographers and al-Naqqash reported. The majority read "khuliqat" with a fatha on the qaf and a damma on the kha'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read "khalaqtu" with a fatha on the kha' and a sukun on the qaf, in the first person verb form. Likewise "rufi'at," "nusibat," and "sutihat" (in the verb forms). Abu Haywa read "ruffi'at, nussibat, and sutthat" with shadda in them. "Nusibat" means: it was established standing in the air, not colliding. The majority read "sutihat" with a light ta'. Harun al-Rashid read "suttihat" with a shadda on the ta' for emphasis, and this is the reading of al-Hasan. The apparent meaning of this verse is that the earth is a flat surface, not a sphere, and this is what the people of knowledge hold. The claim that it is spherical, although it does not diminish any pillar of the Shari'a, is a claim that the scholars of the Shari'a do not affirm.

Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to remind with these signs and their like. Then God, exalted is He, negated that he should be a controller over the people, that is, one who compels them, informs them with arrogance, and dominates them. It is said: "So-and-so dominated us" (tasayțara 'alayna fulan). Some people read "bi-musaytir" with a sin, and some "bi-musaiytir" with a sad. Harun read "bi-musaytar" with a fatha on the ta', and this is the dialect of Tamim. In Arabic speech, in this pattern, there are only "musaytir, mubaytir, mubaiqir, and muhaymin." Among the nouns there are "mudaybir" and "mujaymir," which is the name of a valley. It is possible that these two are diminutives.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except for him who turns away and disbelieves﴾, some interpreters said: "The exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning is: except for him who turns away and disbelieves, then you have control over him. Thus the verse, according to this view, contains no abrogation (naskh)." Others among them said: "The exception is disconnected (istithna' munfasil), and the meaning is: 'You are not a controller over them,' and the statement is complete. It is a verse of truce (ayat muwada'a) abrogated by the sword." Then He said: ﴿Except for him who turns away and disbelieves﴾ ﴿then God will punish him﴾. This is the correct view, because the surah is Meccan, and fighting was revealed only in Medina. "Man" here means "alladhi" (the one who).

Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, Qatada, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "Ala man tawalla" with a fatha on the hamza, in the sense of opening the speech, and "man," according to this reading, is a conditional particle. "Al-'adhab al-akbar" (the greatest punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter, because they had already been punished in this world by hunger, killing and other things. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-innahu yu'adhdhibuhu Allah."

The majority read "iyabahum," a verbal noun from "ab yaoub," meaning he returned, and it is the gathering and the return to God, exalted is He. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "iyyabahum" with a shadda on the ya', on the pattern "fi'al" with a kasra on the fa', its original form being "fay'al," from "a-y-b," a verb whose original form is "fayal." It may also be from "a-w-b," in which case it would be "iwab," and the hamza was eased. In the case of assimilation, the required form would be to restore it as "iwwab," but the ya' was preferred in it, contrary to analogy.

[p. 603] The commentary on Surat [al-Ghashiyah] is complete, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.
